lines.text: Grains and dairy products form the backbone of many diets worldwide. Grains — also called cereals — include wheat, rice, oats, barley, corn (maize), and rye. Wheat is ground into flour, which becomes bread, pasta, pastry, and countless baked goods. Rice is a staple in Asian, Middle Eastern, and African cuisines, available as white rice, brown rice, basmati, and jasmine varieties. Oats are popular for porridge and muesli, while barley is used in soups and stews. Whole grains retain their bran and germ, making them more nutritious than refined grains. Dairy products come from animal milk — primarily cow's milk, but also goat's and sheep's milk. Milk can be full-fat (whole), semi-skimmed, or skimmed. From milk come butter, cream, yoghurt, and an enormous variety of cheeses — from mild cheddar to pungent blue cheese, from soft brie to hard parmesan. Eggs, while not technically dairy, are often grouped alongside dairy products in shops and recipes. Plant-based alternatives have surged in popularity: oat milk, almond milk, soya milk, and coconut yoghurt now fill supermarket shelves alongside traditional dairy. Understanding grain and dairy vocabulary is essential for cooking, shopping, reading food labels, and discussing dietary preferences.

lines.text: Britain produces over 700 named cheeses. Cheddar (from Somerset) is the most famous. Stilton is the 'King of English cheeses' — a blue-veined cheese with protected status. A 'cheeseboard' (selection of cheeses) is a traditional end to a formal British meal.

lines.text: English bread vocabulary is rich: a 'loaf' (whole bread), a 'slice' (cut piece), a 'roll' (small round bread), a 'baguette' (French stick), a 'bun' (sweet roll), 'toast' (grilled bread), 'crumbs' (small pieces). 'Wholemeal' (UK) = 'whole wheat' (US).

lines.text: UK milk is colour-coded: blue cap = whole/full-fat, green cap = semi-skimmed, red cap = skimmed. 'UHT' (long-life) milk doesn't need refrigeration until opened. 'Organic', 'free-range', and 'grass-fed' are common label terms.

lines.text: Plant-based alternatives are mainstream in English-speaking countries. 'Oat milk', 'almond milk', 'soya milk', and 'coconut milk' are standard terms. Note: in some countries, 'milk' can only legally refer to animal milk — alternatives may be labelled 'drink' or 'beverage'.

lines.text: 'Gluten-free' is a widely understood dietary term in English. Gluten is a protein in wheat, barley, and rye. Many restaurants offer gluten-free options. Related vocabulary: 'coeliac disease', 'intolerance', 'allergen', 'free from' (UK label term).
